prompt:
THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS (verbatim — they lead; every skill, asset, place, amount of time and refusal in them binds every route): I have a DJI Mavic 3 and my FAA Part 107 license, I'm in Phoenix. I want to clear $4,500 from drone work in the next 60 days. I can spend $1,500 and I can fly about 20 hours a week.

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $4,500 (USD), collected within 60 day(s).
- Capital: at most $1,500 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: at most 20 hour(s) a week of the owner's own work (about 87 a month), every route's work together. Routes must fit inside it.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 60 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.
- For this goal only, the owner offered their own work ("I can fly about 20 hours a week"): routes the owner personally performs — in person included — are allowed, using only the skills and assets their words state and inside their stated hours. Set performer OWNER and count every one of those hours.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

prompt:
THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS (verbatim — they lead; every skill, asset, place, amount of time and refusal in them binds every route): I have a DJI Mavic 3 and my FAA Part 107 license, I'm in Phoenix. I want to clear $4,500 from drone work in the next 60 days. I can spend $1,500 and I can fly about 20 hours a week.

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $4,500 (USD), collected within 60 day(s).
- Capital: at most $1,500 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: at most 20 hour(s) a week of the owner's own work (about 87 a month), every route's work together. Routes must fit inside it.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 60 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.
- For this goal only, the owner offered their own work ("I can fly about 20 hours a week"): routes the owner personally performs — in person included — are allowed, using only the skills and assets their words state and inside their stated hours. Set performer OWNER and count every one of those hours.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

prompt:
THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS (verbatim — they lead; every skill, asset, place, amount of time and refusal in them binds every route): Seattle. I have zero money to invest and I need $500 within 7 days. I can put in 15 hours this week. Figure out the fastest legit way.

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $500 (USD), collected within 7 day(s).
- Capital: at most $0 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: at most 15 hour(s) of the owner's own work in the whole window. Routes must fit inside it.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 7 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.
- For this goal only, the owner offered their own work ("I can put in 15 hours"): routes the owner personally performs — in person included — are allowed, using only the skills and assets their words state and inside their stated hours. Set performer OWNER and count every one of those hours.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $500 (USD), collected within 7 day(s).
- Capital: at most $0 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: at most 15 hour(s) of the owner's own work in the whole window. Routes must fit inside it.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 7 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.
- For this goal only, the owner offered their own work ("I can put in 15 hours"): routes the owner personally performs — in person included — are allowed, using only the skills and assets their words state and inside their stated hours. Set performer OWNER and count every one of those hours.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

BUILD FROM THE FINDINGS. Start from the real buyer problems, the spending on comparable offers, the reachable channels, the fulfilment options, the costs and the payment terms the findings show, and design routes that use them. A new offer may rest on comparable demand: buyers of this kind shown paying for comparable things now. For every figure, say in "grounds" which finding supports it (its ref), or null where it is your estimate; never cite a finding for a figure it does not state. Set demandScope COMPARABLE when the demand finding is about comparable offers and EXACT only when it shows buyers asking for this very offer. Where a finding contradicts a direction or a route, do not restate it in other words: say in "rethink" what the evidence teaches about the buyer, the offer, the price or the channel, and change the approach accordingly.

STEP 2 — ROUTES. Propose up to 6 concrete commercial routes built from the owner profile and the findings, each able to collect real money for this objective inside every limit above. Each is one whole transaction: a specific kind of buyer who pays, a specific offer, a price such buyers pay today, how they are reached, who delivers it and at what direct cost, how long until the first money settles, and how many such buyers exist. Propose only as many as are genuinely worth researching: one well-founded route is better than several weak ones, routes differ where the owner's means and the evidence point different ways, and no count of buyer kinds (LOCAL_CONSUMER, LOCAL_BUSINESS, ONLINE_MARKETPLACE, ONLINE_CONSUMER, B2B) or mechanisms is required. When the owner names a place, an asset or a hands-on skill, and the target is small or the window short, buyers near them (households and local businesses, reached directly) are usually the fastest money — the in-person work done by the owner where this goal's words offer it, otherwise by a local provider the owner books and pays, as the operating rule above allows: consider them before anything sold to the whole internet. A route that would fit any request equally — a report, an audit, a template, a dashboard, a course or an "AI" product offered to everyone — is a poor route unless the owner's own words point to it. Each route says in ownerFit which of the owner's stated facts it uses.

prompt:
THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS (verbatim — they lead; every skill, asset, place, amount of time and refusal in them binds every route): I want a business that does $20,000 in the next 90 days and keeps going after. I'm in Minneapolis, I have $5,000 to fund it, and I can't put any hours in myself at all, so it has to run without me. Choose whatever you think works.

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $20,000 (USD), collected within 90 day(s).
- Capital: at most $5,000 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: no figure set; the owner does no routine personal work.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 90 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

FINDINGS — what research has established for this goal, each from a source that was read (cite by ref; they are the only facts here):
- F1 [price_evidence] In MHI's fixed panel of 27 DTC brands, Meta ads in Black Friday week 2025 (Nov 24-30) had a median CPA of $50.86 and median ROAS of 1.65 (article dated 2026-10-31; no apparel breakdown). (Black Friday 2025 Meta Ads Benchmarks: Daily CPA, ROAS and Spend Index for DTC B, 2026-10-31)
- F2 [price_evidence] In the same MHI panel, Cyber Monday week 2025 (Dec 1-7) had a median Meta CPA of $50.07 and median ROAS of 1.74. (Black Friday 2025 Meta Ads Benchmarks, 2026-10-31)
- F3 [price_evidence] Across all qualifying brands (37) in MHI's data, Black Friday week 2025 had the quarter's lowest median Meta CPA at $44.00. (Black Friday 2025 Meta Ads Benchmarks, 2026-10-31)
- F4 [cost_evidence] Lebesgue (2026-10-16): among its biggest Meta spenders, the median brand paid 59% more CPM in Black Friday week 2025 than in September 2025. (Are Meta Ads Worth It on Black Friday? CPM and ROAS Data, 2026-10-16)
- F5 [cost_evidence] Lebesgue (2026-10-16): Meta CPMs for Cyber week 2025 averaged 31% above September 2025. (Are Meta Ads Worth It on Black Friday? CPM and ROAS Data, 2026-10-16)
- F6 [timing] Printful's average fulfillment time is 2-5 business days for all products (Printful shipping page, fetched 2026-11-26). (Printful Shipping, 2026-11-26)

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $20,000 (USD), collected within 90 day(s).
- Capital: at most $5,000 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: no figure set; the owner does no routine personal work.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 90 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- This operation is run entirely online, with AI and software doing as much of the work as possible: the owner does no physical work — no travel, no deliveries, no distributing anything, no meeting customers, no performing a service and no running a physical operation. Work that is physical is still in scope when an independent supplier or subcontractor performs it and this operation coordinates it remotely, as a broker, referrer or subcontracting coordinator. Look in every country and region: where the buyers are is a business choice made on demand, margin, fulfilment access, how fast money settles, competition and how much can be automated — never on where the owner lives.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer

BUILD FROM THE FINDINGS. Start from the real buyer problems, the spending on comparable offers, the reachable channels, the fulfilment options, the costs and the payment terms the findings show, and design routes that use them. A new offer may rest on comparable demand: buyers of this kind shown paying for comparable things now. For every figure, say in "grounds" which finding supports it (its ref), or null where it is your estimate; never cite a finding for a figure it does not state. Set demandScope COMPARABLE when the demand finding is about comparable offers and EXACT only when it shows buyers asking for this very offer. Where a finding contradicts a direction or a route, do not restate it in other words: say in "rethink" what the evidence teaches about the buyer, the offer, the price or the channel, and change the approach accordingly.

STEP 2 — ROUTES. Propose up to 6 concrete commercial routes built from the owner profile and the findings, each able to collect real money for this objective inside every limit above. Each is one whole transaction: a specific kind of buyer who pays, a specific offer, a price such buyers pay today, how they are reached, who delivers it and at what direct cost, how long until the first money settles, and how many such buyers exist. Propose only as many as are genuinely worth researching: one well-founded route is better than several weak ones, routes differ where the owner's means and the evidence point different ways, and no count of buyer kinds (LOCAL_CONSUMER, LOCAL_BUSINESS, ONLINE_MARKETPLACE, ONLINE_CONSUMER, B2B) or mechanisms is required. prompt:
THE OWNER'S OWN WORDS (verbatim — they lead; every skill, asset, place, amount of time and refusal in them binds every route): I have a DJI Mavic 3 and my FAA Part 107 license, I'm in Phoenix. I want to clear $4,500 from drone work in the next 60 days. I can spend $1,500 and I can fly about 20 hours a week.

STEP 1 — READ THE OWNER. Before any route, write in "owner" what those words say about: skills (what they can do, languages they speak), assets (equipment, a vehicle, space, accounts, an audience, contacts), location, hours (and when they are free), capital, and refusals. Write "not stated" for anything the words do not say; never invent it.

DATE: Today is 2026-11-26 (late November). Use the season and the calendar where the owner and the buyers are — weather, holidays, school terms, year-end budgets and closures — when choosing buyers, channels and timing, and keep any constraint the owner set for part of the window.

LIMITS (hard rules):
- The money still needed: $4,500 (USD), collected within 60 day(s), by 25 January 2027.
- Capital: at most $1,500 may be tied up before money comes back. A route needing more is not allowed.
- Owner's time: at most 20 hour(s) a week of the owner's own work (about 87 a month), every route's work together. Routes must fit inside it.
- Time: the first money must settle inside 60 day(s). A buyer who pays in arrears, on invoice terms or after a long sales cycle that would land later is not allowed.
- No industry is excluded: choose on economics, time to cash and whether it can be done.
- For this goal the owner offered their own work ("I can fly about 20 hours a week"), so the standing rule that the owner does no physical work does not apply to it: routes the owner personally performs — in person, deliveries, shifts, gigs and services included — are allowed, inside their stated hours, using the skills and assets their words state or work that needs no particular skill, licence or equipment they did not state. Set performer OWNER and count every one of those hours. Work can also be done by an independent supplier or subcontractor that this operation coordinates, and AI and software should do as much of the remaining work as possible.

FEASIBILITY (every route must pass every one):
- uses what the owner said they have — skills, assets, location, free time — or a priced subcontractor; never expertise the owner did not claim, and never a menu that would fit any request; when the owner states a licence, certification or trade, at least one route sells that licensed or trade work itself to the buyers who pay for it, rather than only products around it
- the first money settles inside the window
- the channel produces paying buyers inside the window with the stated budget: a channel that compounds slowly (search ranking, a new content or video channel, a newsletter, a course, a new marketplace profile with no reviews, enterprise procurement) cannot do that in a short window, and paid advertising needs a budget that buys enough reach to close the sales needed
- a named fulfiller with a known cost who can start now: the owner, within the stated hours and skills they actually have; a subcontractor whose price fits the capital; or Brain, only for a deliverable it has proved
- the price is anchored to what this kind of buyer typically pays for this today; commodity work is priced at its market rate, never far above it; the buyer count is built from the bottom up (a place, a directory, a marketplace category), never a top-down guess
- the capital is read as the owner gave it: a small budget rules out spend-heavy channels; a large one may fund inventory, equipment or paid labour where that is what earns the money; few owner hours rule out labour-per-unit work that does not scale; a recurring target needs recurring billing
- the market exists and is buying now, in this season; no invented or dead markets
- the owner's side adds something the buyer pays for: reselling gigs, services or products another platform already sells to the same buyers at a markup, or a referral commission without a named partner programme that publishes what it pays, is not a route; a digital deliverable a model would generate (templates, reports, scripts, graphics, newsletters, "AI" content) is not a route unless a named kind of buyer is already shown paying for exactly that
- lawful, and inside the terms of every platform it uses: nothing deceptive (fake, paid or incentivised reviews, fake engagement or testimonials), nothing that breaks a marketplace's or platform's rules, no licensed work done without the licence, and no regulated claim made without the right to make it
- every figure that cites a finding says what that finding says, for buyers like these; a route a finding contradicts is not proposed again in another wording; with findings available, a route resting on none of them is weaker than one that rests on them; demand shown only for comparable offers is comparable demand, never proof that buyers want this exact offer
